moderate: Brazil's 2.6% current account deficit is larger than the 1.5-2% pre-pandemic average, and the shortfall in March's trade surplus ($6.41 billion vs $7.40 billion consensus) signals that rising energy costs will keep the deficit wide through year-end.
At 2.6% of GDP, the deficit reflects both goods trade pressure (the March shortfall) and large profit repatriation from multinational firms, making it a structural constraint on monetary easing.

The current account deficit at 2.6% GDP means Brazil needs the 12% policy rate to keep the USD/BRL at 5.01, because lower rates would push the currency weaker and widen the deficit as import prices rise.
expert: Brazil's 2.6% current account deficit, combined with the March trade surplus miss, signals that the economy is losing competitiveness as energy import costs offset commodity export gains, creating a structural headwind that will prevent the central bank from cutting rates below 10% without triggering a depreciation spiral.

At 2.6% deficit with USD/BRL at 5.01, the external position is stable only because the 12% real rate is attractive to foreign investors, but this creates a policy trap where any cuts below 10% risk a sharp depreciation that would import inflation.

The current account deficit of 2.6% GDP, combined with the 6.7% fiscal deficit, means Brazil's external imbalance is being financed by attracting foreign capital at 13.80% yields, a dynamic that will unwind sharply if the central bank cuts rates faster than the Fed or if confidence deteriorates further from the current 49.22 level.

beginner: The central bank raised rates to 12% to fight inflation, but this high rate is crushing the economy (growth at 1.7%) and consumer confidence (49.22), so traders expect cuts to start soon.

At 12%, the policy rate is one of the highest in the world, which means borrowing costs for mortgages and business loans are painful, but the central bank believes it needs this pain to bring inflation down from where it was.
The April 28-29 Copom decision will tell you if the central bank is ready to start cutting, and markets are betting it will, but the 4.2% inflation rate and 6.7% deficit mean cuts will come slowly.
moderate: Brazil's 12% policy rate is at cycle peak, and the April 28-29 Copom decision is the inflection point where the central bank must choose between holding steady (risking recession) or cutting to prevent growth collapse.

At 12%, the real rate is 7.8% after accounting for 4.2% inflation, making it one of the highest real rates in the world, which explains why the inverted yield curve at -140bps is signaling a recession.

The 12% rate has delivered inflation down from 10%+ in 2022, but the 6.5% unemployment and 49.22 confidence reading suggest the economy is losing momentum faster than the central bank can cut safely given the 6.7% fiscal deficit.
expert: Brazil's 12% policy rate sits at a cycle peak with the real rate at 7.8%, and the April Copom meeting is the critical signal for whether the central bank will cut 50bps (market base case) or hold steady, with cuts dependent on core inflation tracking below 3.8% by May.

At 12%, the policy rate is suppressing growth to 1.7% while the 140bps inverted curve signals the market is pricing in a 75bps cut cycle by year-end, but the 6.7% deficit and 2.6% current account imbalance mean the central bank cannot cut faster than 50bps per meeting without risking a depreciation spiral.

The 12% rate combined with a 13.80% 10Y yield and negative 140bps curve creates a tightening bias that will force a recession unless the April Copom initiates a clear cutting cycle, but the current account deficit and fiscal imbalance mean the central bank must coordinate with fiscal authorities to prevent capital flight during the easing period.

beginner: Brazilian stocks are up 22.9% this year in local currency, a strong gain that shows investors believe the central bank will start cutting rates soon and confidence will recover.
The stock market rally tells you that despite the 49.22 confidence reading and 1.7% growth, traders are betting the economy will improve, probably because they expect rate cuts to start in April.
Stocks up 22.9% but up only 13.88% in dollar terms means the Brazilian currency has lost value, which is why foreign investors are not getting the full benefit of the stock rally.
moderate: Brazilian stocks gained 22.9% YTD in reais, outperforming a weak global backdrop, because investors are pricing in the April 28-29 Copom decision as the turning point toward rate cuts and improving growth.
The 22.9% gain contrasts sharply with confidence at 49.22, revealing a disconnect where the market is front-running a policy pivot while households remain pessimistic about their personal situations.

In dollar terms, the 13.88% return shows that the real has depreciated against the USD despite the 12% policy rate, a sign that foreign investors are nervous about Brazil's external imbalances and rate cut timing.
expert: Brazilian equities rallied 22.9% in reais (13.88% in USD) on market conviction that the April Copom will cut 50bps and signal a full easing cycle, but this rally is highly sensitive to execution risk if the central bank holds steady or cuts only 25bps.

The 22.9% YTD return reflects a compressed valuation base where Brazilian stocks traded at 7-8x forward earnings heading into 2026, meaning the rally is front-running a narrow window (April decision) to reset the interest rate regime.

With stocks up 22.9% and the inverted curve at 140bps, the market is pricing a 6-7 rate cut cycle (75-100bps total by year-end), but this outcome is contingent on the central bank's ability to cut without triggering a currency crisis, which requires fiscal consolidation or external support that has not yet materialized.

beginner: The 10-year bond yield at 13.80% is very high because investors do not trust that Brazil will control its inflation and deficits, so they demand a big reward for holding the debt.
At 13.80%, the yield is one reason businesses cannot borrow cheaply to invest, which explains why growth is stuck at 1.7%.

Bond yields this high tell you that markets think the central bank will struggle to cut rates quickly, even if inflation comes down, because the 6.7% deficit means bond supply will keep yields elevated.
moderate: Brazil's 13.80% 10Y yield sits 200+ basis points above US equivalents, pricing in both Brazil's 4.2% inflation premium and a 6.7% fiscal deficit that will require sustained high rates to finance.

The yield at 13.80% represents a decline from 14.5% earlier in 2026, but the April Copom decision will be critical, because if the central bank cuts while inflation stays above 4%, yields could spike back to 14.5% or higher.

At 13.80%, the 10Y yield is the central bank's real constraint, because any aggressive rate cutting cycle will cause the yield to rise (as happened in 2021-2022), forcing the central bank to stop cutting and extend monetary tightening.
expert: Brazil's 13.80% 10Y yield reflects a fiscal sustainability panic where the 6.7% deficit and 2.6% current account imbalance create a dual deficit dynamic that bond markets are pricing at a 200bps inflation risk premium plus a 150bps fiscal risk premium.

At 13.80%, the yield is pricing in a scenario where the April Copom cuts 50bps, but the central bank cannot move faster than 50bps per meeting (100bps total by year-end) without triggering a yield spike to 14.5%+ and forcing a policy reversal.

The 10Y yield at 13.80% with the policy rate at 12% implies bond markets expect the real policy rate to fall only 80bps over the next year, a shallow easing cycle that will limit growth upside, meaning equities' 22.9% YTD rally is pricing a scenario that bond markets are currently rejecting.

beginner: The yield curve is inverted at negative 140 basis points, meaning short-term rates are much higher than long-term rates, which is a warning sign that the economy is headed for trouble.
An inverted curve tells you that traders are betting the central bank will have to cut rates sharply soon, because otherwise the economy will slide into recession.
This inversion is one reason consumer confidence collapsed to 49.22, because households and businesses sense that an economic slowdown is coming.
moderate: Brazil's negative 140bps yield curve is one of the steepest inversions in emerging markets, signaling that the market is pricing a severe growth shock if the central bank maintains the 12% policy rate much longer.
The inversion at 140bps is extreme compared to Brazil's historical norms (curves are typically positive), which means traders see a high risk of recession if rate cuts do not begin immediately.

An inverted curve combined with growth at 1.7% and unemployment at 6.5% is a rare signal, typically seen only 6-9 months before a recession, meaning the April Copom's signaling will determine whether the curve re-steepens (bullish) or stays inverted (recession warning).
expert: Brazil's negative 140bps curve reflects a market pricing of 75-100bps in cuts from the 12% policy rate by year-end, with the April Copom decision as the signal point for whether the central bank will deliver on market expectations or shock by holding steady.

At 140bps inverted, the curve is pricing a scenario where real rates must fall to 7% or below to prevent a growth shock, but the 6.7% fiscal deficit and 13.80% 10Y yield constrain how much the central bank can ease before bond markets push yields higher.

The negative 140bps curve combined with growth at 1.7% creates a time-constrained policy environment where the central bank has only 2-3 quarters to stabilize growth through rate cuts before the yield curve inversion forces a sudden policy reversal, likely triggered by capital flight risk.

beginner: The Brazilian real is trading at 5.01 per dollar, which means it has weakened from around 4.70 a few years ago, making imports more expensive and contributing to inflation pressure.
At 5.01, the exchange rate tells you that foreign investors are nervous about Brazil, because they would not demand so many reais for their dollars if they were confident in the economy.
A weaker real is one reason inflation stays sticky at 4.2%, because energy and other imports become more expensive when the currency falls.
moderate: Brazil's USD/BRL at 5.01 has held relatively stable despite the 12% policy rate, a sign that the rate is barely high enough to attract foreign capital given the 6.7% fiscal deficit and 2.6% current account imbalance.

The exchange rate at 5.01 sits near the middle of the 4.90-5.10 range it has traded in 2026, suggesting that the 12% rate is pricing in a defensive equilibrium where any rate cuts below 11% would trigger a move toward 5.20-5.30.
At 5.01, the real remains about 6% weaker than where it traded in 2021, a structural adjustment reflecting Brazil's loss of competitiveness and the gap between Brazilian and US interest rates.
expert: Brazil's USD/BRL at 5.01 is hovering near a critical level where the 12% policy rate is just sufficient to stabilize the currency, and any April Copom cut to 11.50% would likely trigger depreciation toward 5.15-5.25 unless the central bank signals a shallow (total 75bps) cutting cycle.

At 5.01 with a 300bps policy rate differential (Brazil 12% vs US 4.75%), the exchange rate is pricing a scenario where the central bank cuts 50bps per meeting for two meetings (100bps total) but then pauses, but if cuts accelerate to 75bps per meeting, depreciation to 5.30+ becomes inevitable.

The USD/BRL rate at 5.01 is the key constraint on the April Copom's cutting flexibility, because the 2.6% current account deficit and 6.7% fiscal deficit mean Brazil cannot afford to let the real weaken to 5.30+ without triggering an inflation spike through higher import costs and a potential capital flight spiral.

beginner: Brazilian stocks gained 13.88% in dollar terms this year, a solid return but significantly less than the 22.9% gain in local currency, because the real weakened against the dollar.

For a US investor, the 13.88% return tells you that the Brazilian stock market rally has been partly offset by currency losses, making the true return less attractive than it looks to someone investing in reais.
The difference between 22.9% (local) and 13.88% (dollars) of roughly 9 percentage points shows how much the real has depreciated, which makes Brazilian stocks riskier for foreign investors.
moderate: Brazilian stocks returned 13.88% in USD terms, underperforming the 22.9% local return by 900 basis points due to real depreciation from 4.80 to 5.01, showing that foreign investors are bearing currency risk even as the equity market rallies.

The 13.88% USD return compares poorly to emerging market peers (MSCI EM up mid-to-high teens in USD), indicating that the Brazilian rally has been a local story driven by rate cut expectations rather than a broad EM movement.

For foreign investors, the 13.88% return requires holding both Brazilian equity risk and currency depreciation risk, a combination that only works if the April Copom delivers rate cuts and the real stabilizes above 5.00.
expert: Brazilian equities gained 13.88% in USD terms (22.9% in BRL) as the real depreciated from 4.80 to 5.01, creating a two-way bet where foreign investors are implicitly short BRL through their equity exposure and will face severe headwinds if the April Copom signals a shallower cutting cycle than the market is pricing.

The 13.88% USD return reflects a market conviction that rate cuts plus currency stabilization will drive a rally, but this scenario requires the April Copom to cut 50bps and the real to hold above 5.00, a narrow window that breaks if the central bank hesitates or fiscal concerns escalate.

At 13.88% in USD returns with the real at 5.01, foreign investors are effectively taking a leveraged bet on the April Copom decision and the sustainability of Brazil's external position, meaning a shock (no cut, or fiscal deterioration forcing yields higher) could trigger a sharp reversal to 5.20+ and wipe out the year's gains.

beginner: Brazil's trade surplus fell short of expectations in March because energy imports are eating the profits from higher oil prices. Brazil is supposed to be winning from expensive oil, but it is losing anyway.
Consumer confidence crashed to 49 because people are terrified of inflation. The central bank is charging 15% to borrow money, and families are pulling back.
Rising energy costs plus weak consumer demand is a trap. Exports slow, inflation persists, and the central bank has to keep rates sky-high.
moderate: March trade surplus at $6.41 billion missed consensus at $7.40 billion, not because exports fell but because energy imports surged. Brazil is a net energy exporter, so higher crude should help, but global crude is being disrupted and Brazil's import bill is rising faster than export revenues. Consumer confidence at 49.22 reflects the reality: the central bank's 15% policy rate is destroying household demand and the Copom faces a credibility crisis.

CPI at 3.81% in February sits inside the target band, but it is rising. The central bank held the policy rate at 15% in February and has not cut since December, signaling no relief coming. Compare this to India, which can afford to wait for inflation to fall because external shocks are managed. Brazil cannot wait because every month of 15% rates crushes growth and consumer confidence further.

The April 28-29 Copom decision is the fulcrum. Inflation expectations are drifting, unemployment is low at 5.8%, and the real effective exchange rate is depreciating. If Copom cuts 50 basis points, it signals confidence inflation will stabilize and the currency can weaken in a controlled manner. If it holds or hikes, growth for 2026 undershoots the 1.7% forecast and capital flows out.
expert: Trade surplus at $6.41 billion versus $7.40 billion consensus reflects rising energy import costs offsetting export strength. CPI at 3.81%, policy rate at 15%, and consumer confidence at 49.22 signal a central bank trapped between inflation expectations drift and demand destruction. The Copom has not cut since December and the market prices two cuts this year against a backdrop of sticky core inflation.

Directional signal: the 15% policy rate is unsustainable politically and economically, but cutting into 3.81% inflation with rising energy costs is a gamble. The April 28-29 Copom decision will reveal whether the central bank believes inflation is anchored or slipping. A 50 basis point cut signals confidence; a hold signals panic about pass-through from energy and currency weakness.

Forward implication: if energy import costs stay elevated and Copom cuts in April, the real effective exchange rate will weaken further, imported inflation accelerates, and the central bank faces a second-half repricing of terminal rate expectations. If Copom holds at 15%, the 1.7% growth forecast is at risk and capital flight accelerates. Watch March CPI print (due April 11) and the April 28 Copom decision. A 50 basis point cut plus stable inflation expectations would stabilize the outlook; a hold at 15% means the 2026 growth forecast falls to 1.0% or lower.

fxRegime.label: Managed Float
fxRegime.beginner: Brazil’s real floats freely on currency markets, but the central bank (BCB) steps in when moves become extreme. USD/BRL shows how many reais you need to buy one US dollar. At 5.22, one dollar costs about 5.2 reais. Brazil’s very high interest rates attract foreign investors seeking better returns — this is called a ‘carry trade’ — which can support the real, but political or fiscal worries can cause sharp sell-offs.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float with active BCB intervention via FX swaps (NDF-settled) and spot auctions. The real is one of the most traded EM currencies, driven by: the Selic-Fed funds differential (~11pp, supporting carry), commodity exposure (soybeans, iron ore, oil), and fiscal/political risk sentiment. BRL vol (~16-17% annualized) reflects the tension between attractive carry and periodic fiscal/political risk-off episodes.
fxRegime.expert: Managed float with intervention primarily via USD-settled FX swap programme (notional ~$100bn outstanding) rather than spot reserves. BCB uses swaps to manage forward curve steepness and hedge corporate external debt rollover risk. Reserve position ~$350bn provides ample cover (~14 months imports) and exceeds Guidotti-Greenspan threshold. Key BRL dynamics: (1) carry attractiveness — Selic-SOFR spread ~11pp supports positioning but creates convex downside risk on unwind; (2) terms of trade — BRL correlated with commodity index (~0.5) given export mix (soybeans, iron ore, oil, protein); (3) fiscal risk premium — pre-election spending risk and debt trajectory keep the BRL risk premium elevated vs model-implied fair value.

GDP Growth.beginner: Brazil's economy is benefiting from the oil price surge, as Petrobras produces large amounts of oil and the higher prices mean more revenue for the company and the Brazilian government — but high interest rates at home are still a brake on overall economic growth.
GDP Growth.moderate: Brazil's GDP growth benefits from higher Petrobras revenues and agricultural export strength (soybeans, corn), but is constrained by the world's highest real interest rates (Selic above 13%), fiscal concerns under President Lula, and a BRL that has been weakening on risk-off sentiment despite improving terms of trade.
GDP Growth.expert: Brazil's growth is caught between two opposing forces: the commodity export windfall (oil, agriculture) improving the external accounts and Petrobras fiscal contributions, and the Lula government's fiscal expansion tendencies that have kept the Selic elevated as the BCB resists easing that could trigger FX depreciation and BRL-denominated inflation.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Brazilian inflation has been stubbornly high, partly because of the weak currency and partly because of rising food prices, and higher oil prices from the Iran conflict could push fuel and goods prices higher, adding to cost-of-living pressure.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Brazilian CPI has been running above the BCB's 3% target amid BRL weakness (FX passthrough) and food price pressures; the Iran oil shock creates upside CPI risk via domestic fuel prices (Petrobras pricing policy) and logistics costs — but Petrobras's pricing formula may absorb some of the shock if the government exercises its shareholder influence to delay passthrough.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Brazil's inflation dynamics are fundamentally linked to the BRL exchange rate via FX passthrough (estimated at 0.2-0.3pp of CPI per 10% BRL depreciation); the Iran risk-off environment that typically weakens BRL creates a secondary inflationary impulse on top of direct energy price increases; any signal of political interference in BCB independence would amplify both BRL weakness and inflationary expectations.

Unemployment.beginner: Brazil's unemployment rate has been falling to around 6.5-7%, relatively low by historical standards, helped by growth in agriculture, construction, and services — though quality jobs with social benefits remain scarce for many workers.
Unemployment.moderate: Brazil's unemployment at ~6.5% is at a cyclical low, supported by agricultural employment (record harvests) and government-linked construction projects; the oil price windfall could support Petrobras employment and supply-chain jobs in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo states, partially offsetting any weakening in manufacturing from BRL volatility.
Unemployment.expert: Brazil's labour market is structurally characterised by high informality (40%+ of the workforce), which creates a buffer against cyclical shocks (informal workers absorb adjustment without appearing in unemployment statistics) but limits productivity growth and wage-setting efficiency; the oil-related employment boost is concentrated in formal high-wage jobs (Petrobras, engineering services) with limited aggregate demand multiplier effects for the broader economy.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Brazil's government is spending more than it earns, with a persistent fiscal deficit, and investors worry that the Lula government may expand spending further — which could weaken the currency and push up inflation.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Brazil's fiscal deficit (primary + interest: near 7-8% of GDP on consolidated basis) reflects the fundamental tension between constitutional spending mandates, social program expansion, and debt dynamics; Petrobras dividends (boosted by high oil prices) provide incremental fiscal revenue, but the structural spending trajectory remains unsustainable without reform.
Budget Deficit.expert: Brazil's fiscal framework is constrained by constitutional spending rules and the BCB's inflation target mandate; the Petrobras dividend windfall at $90+ oil provides a one-time fiscal improvement estimated at R$30-50bn (additional 0.3-0.5% of GDP) that could temporarily reduce the primary deficit — but this does not alter the structural deficit dynamic that requires entitlement reform the Lula government has been reluctant to pursue before elections.

Current Account.beginner: Brazil is becoming a larger oil exporter, and the surge in oil prices means the country is earning significantly more from its energy exports — improving the trade balance and potentially supporting the Brazilian real.
Current Account.moderate: Brazil's current account is improving mechanically from higher Petrobras oil export revenues at $90+ WTI; the agricultural export surplus (soybeans, corn at elevated prices) provides additional support; but Brazil's structural current account deficit from services means the improvement may be smaller than commodity price movements suggest.
Current Account.expert: Brazil's oil export capacity is growing structurally as Santos Basin pre-salt developments ramp up; at $90+ WTI, Brazilian breakeven costs of $35-40/barrel generate extraordinary economic rent; the key risk is that Lula government shareholder pressure on Petrobras's fuel pricing policy (to limit domestic inflation) could reduce Petrobras's upstream profitability and dividend capacity, partially negating the fiscal windfall from higher global prices.

Policy Rate.beginner: Brazil has some of the world's highest interest rates, with the Selic rate above 13%, making borrowing extremely expensive — and the central bank has been cautious about cutting rates because of persistent inflation and currency weakness.
Policy Rate.moderate: Brazil's Selic rate above 13% reflects the BCB's response to persistent inflation and BRL weakness; the Iran shock creates conflicting signals for the BCB: higher oil-driven CPI argues for holding, but positive terms-of-trade improvement (oil revenues) argues for easing; the risk-off BRL depreciation typically tips the BCB toward holding to defend currency credibility.
Policy Rate.expert: Brazil's real interest rate (Selic minus CPI) is among the world's highest, creating a significant competitiveness cost for the domestic economy; the BCB's rate-setting is constrained by the constant threat of capital outflows if real rates fall too quickly toward EM peer levels; the Iran shock that strengthens the current account (higher oil exports) but weakens the capital account (risk-off outflows) creates net BOP uncertainty the BCB will resolve by keeping rates elevated — effectively exporting the real income cost of the oil shock to Brazilian households and businesses through tight monetary conditions.

beginner: Russia grew at 1.2% in early 2026, but that's about to slow down hard as oil prices stabilize and war costs drain the budget.
Growth of 1.2% sounds okay until you remember Russia needs 2-3% just to avoid recession, so this is already the beginning of trouble.
The economy is running on fumes from oil revenues and forced labor substitution, which works for a few quarters but cannot sustain 1.2% growth when both inputs fade.
moderate: At 1.2% growth with a 12.5% policy rate, Russia is burning purchasing power to stay afloat, a trap that worked in 2022-2023 but breaks down when growth falls below 0.8% as forecasts expect.
Oil prices above $80 per barrel are masking a structural collapse: the current account surplus of 2% GDP and capital controls are what keep the ruble from collapsing, not real economic expansion.

Compare this to 2021 when Russia grew 4.7% with a 4.25% rate and $60 oil: the economy has become dependent on external shocks (war, sanctions relief, commodity supercycles) rather than productivity, making 1.2% unsustainable once oil normalizes.
expert: GDP growth at 1.2% YoY reflects carryover from 2025's 3.0% surge but masks a quarterly deceleration to roughly 0.3-0.5% run rate, signaling the 0.8% 2026 forecast is already materializing.

With the central bank holding the policy rate at 12.5%, real interest rates (nominal minus expected inflation of 4.7%) sit at 7.8%, crowding out private investment and forcing growth toward zero-sum military production and consumption.

Watch credit growth: if ruble credit expansion slows below 5% QoQ while USD/RUB stays above 75, the economy has hit the wall on domestic demand, and 1.2% will drop to 0.5% by Q3 2026 regardless of oil.

beginner: Inflation at 4.7% sounds controlled, but Russia's 12.5% interest rate exists because the central bank does not trust that number.
Prices are being held down by capital controls and supply rationing, not by actual price stability, so when those controls slip (they always do), inflation rips back to 8-10% within months.
The gap between the policy rate and inflation tells you everything: the central bank is betting that pain now prevents catastrophe later, but that bet only works if oil stays above $75.
moderate: CPI at 4.7% is artificially low because price controls on food and energy mask true inflation running closer to 7-8% on tradable goods, a pattern Russia has run since 2022 sanctions.

The central bank's 12.5% rate (the highest in the world outside Venezuela and Zimbabwe) indicates inflation expectations are still unanchored, with households and firms pricing in 6-8% despite the 4.7% headline number.

In 2022, Russia reported 11% inflation while holding rates at 14%, a nearly identical real rate regime; today's 4.7% with 12.5% rates suggests either deflation fears (unlikely) or that central bankers see demand destruction already arriving.
expert: Headline CPI at 4.7% masks core inflation running 5.5-6.2% based on non-food, non-energy components, a 70-150bps gap that indicates food price controls are the sole restraint on the official number.

The central bank's implicit inflation target appears to be 5-6%, not the stated 4%, given that 12.5% rates should drive inflation toward 2-3% in a normal regime; the persistence of 4.7% signals either statistical gimmickry or demand is already collapsing faster than the central bank admits.

Monitor M2 growth (last reported at 16-18% YoY): if that accelerates above 20% while CPI stays at 4.7%, the central bank is losing control of expectations, and inflation will spike to 7%+ in Q3 2026 once oil supply shocks hit.

beginner: Unemployment at 2.5% means almost nobody is officially out of work, but that's because the government is drafting men into the army and paying them to fight, not because there are lots of normal jobs.
Real unemployment (people who want work but cannot find it) is probably 2-3x higher, hidden in military conscription, forced state employment, and people who gave up looking.
When the war ends or recruitment stops, this number will explode, so watch it as a leading indicator of how much economic pain is being deferred.
moderate: At 2.5%, Russia's unemployment sits at levels last seen in 2012, before the first Ukraine invasion, but the composition is entirely different: conscription has replaced normal labor market competition, making the rate a political fiction rather than an economic measure.

Compare to pre-2022 when 5.3% unemployment coexisted with labor shortages; today, 2.5% coexists with widespread worker shortages in civilian sectors (retail, healthcare, agriculture) and wage inflation of 8-10%, evidence that the labor market is not tight by supply-and-demand but by forcible removal of workers.
The parallel economy of conscription, military spending, and war-related employment masks true cyclical unemployment, which remains at roughly 3.5-4.5% beneath the official rate.
expert: Unemployment at 2.5% reflects roughly 1.8-2.0 million persons officially registered as unemployed out of a 72+ million labor force, but conscription of 500k-600k annually since 2022 has artificially suppressed the rate by an estimated 150-200bps.

Labor force participation has dropped 1.2 percentage points since 2021 (from 63.8% to 62.6%), with women and youth comprising the bulk of exits, indicating that the true slack in the labor market is hidden in discouraged worker flows rather than unemployment stocks.

If military demobilization begins (contingent on peace talks), expect unemployment to spike to 4.5-5.5% within two quarters as conscripted workers re-enter civilian labor markets, a shock that will force the central bank to cut rates below 10% and trigger stagflationary dynamics that extend the 0.8% growth forecast downward.

beginner: Russia's budget deficit is 2.5% of GDP, meaning the government spends 2.5% more than it takes in each year, and that gap is being filled by oil revenues and financial repression (forcing banks to hold government debt).

That does not sound huge compared to other countries, but Russia has almost no debt markets left (sanctions), so the deficit must be covered by printing money or taking it from the central bank, which fuels inflation.
Watch this number: if oil falls to $60, the deficit could hit 4-5% of GDP overnight, forcing the central bank to either print money (inflation) or slash spending (recession).
moderate: The 2.5% deficit reported in early 2026 excludes off-budget spending on defense and secret programs, with true military/security spending likely running 6-7% of GDP (compared to official defense budgets of 5.4%), meaning the true fiscal deficit is closer to 4-5% of GDP.

Oil revenues account for roughly 40-45% of federal budget receipts and 70%+ of foreign exchange earnings, so the deficit math is entirely dependent on oil prices above $75-80, a condition that became more fragile in April 2026 as OPEC+ signals output increases.

Compare to 2021 when the deficit was negative (surplus of 1.8% of GDP) with oil at $65-70: the 2.5% deficit today signals that war spending has overwhelmed oil revenue gains, and when crude normalizes below $75, the budget will swing toward 3-4% deficit within one quarter.
expert: The 2.5% deficit (roughly 3.5 trillion rubles, or $46 billion at 76 RUB/USD) is being financed through a mix of forced central bank purchases (estimated 30-40%), domestic banking system absorption via capital requirements (35-40%), and a residual of export earnings retained by the central bank; the structure is not sustainable if oil falls below $75.

Off-budget defense spending adds an estimated 1.5-2.0 percentage points to the fiscal deficit, implying a true general government deficit of 4.0-4.5% of GDP, a level that in normal circumstances would trigger currency depreciation, but sanctions-driven capital controls and FX surrender requirements mask the imbalance.

If oil averages $65-70 in Q2-Q3 2026 (a 10-15% decline from current $80+ levels), the federal budget deficit will mechanically widen to 4-5% of GDP, forcing either a 200-300bps hike in the policy rate (economic collapse) or monetization (inflation spike to 8-10%), both of which truncate the 1.2% growth forecast to negative territory by mid-year.

beginner: Russia has a 2% current account surplus, meaning it sells more to the world than it buys, which sounds good until you realize it is mostly oil and gas that gets sold, not manufactured goods with long-term jobs.

A 2% surplus is strong, but it exists only because of sanctions: normally, Russians would spend more on imports, and that 2% would shrink to 0-0.5%, showing that the surplus is forced scarcity, not real wealth.
Watch the oil price: every $10 drop in oil prices cuts the current account surplus by roughly 0.5% of GDP, so if oil falls to $65, the surplus disappears and the ruble comes under pressure.
moderate: The 2% current account surplus of 2026 represents roughly $40-45 billion in annual inflows, with oil and gas accounting for 75-80% of export revenue; compare this to 2021 when the surplus was 2.1% despite lower oil prices because capital flows were open and imports were unrestricted.

The surplus today is entirely a function of import collapse (down 30-40% since 2021) due to sanctions and currency controls, not export strength: real exports ex-energy have fallen 15-20%, indicating that the current account strength is a mirage of demand destruction.

Ukraine war spending requires dollar outflows that offset the trade surplus, with estimates of $10-15 billion annually in uncompensated military aid and war losses; the true current account (including capital transfers) is likely 0.5-1.0% of GDP, not 2.0%.
expert: The current account surplus of 2% GDP (roughly $45-50 billion annually) breaks down as follows: crude oil and refined products ($90-100 billion), natural gas ($20-25 billion, down 60% from 2021 due to pipeline cuts), minerals and metals ($25-30 billion), and non-commodity exports ($35-40 billion, mostly down-market chemicals and machinery).

Capital controls and FX surrender requirements (central bank purchase of 50% of enterprise foreign exchange earnings) artificially suppress imports and inflate the apparent current account surplus; adjusting for these distortions, the economic current account (the value that would flow if markets were open) sits at 0.5-0.8% of GDP.

If oil falls to $65 (a 20% decline from current levels) and LNG exports remain impaired by sanctions, the current account surplus will compress to 0.5% GDP by Q3 2026; combined with military outflows and a potential capital account reversal if sanctions ease, the central bank's FX reserve accumulation will stall, forcing either a 10-15% ruble devaluation or a policy rate increase above 14%, both tail risks for the 1.2% growth forecast.

beginner: The central bank is holding interest rates at 12.5%, the highest level since 2022, because inflation expectations are still unstable and the ruble keeps weakening when they cut.
At 12.5%, borrowing money is painfully expensive for businesses and households, so investment and consumption collapse, which drags down growth even though it slows inflation.

The central bank is betting that pain now (high unemployment, failed startups) prevents hyperinflation later, but if oil prices fall or war costs explode, that bet loses and rates will have to stay high until growth turns negative.
moderate: The 12.5% policy rate is the highest in the world among major economies (and comparable only to Venezuela and Zimbabwe), indicating that the central bank views ruble depreciation and inflation expectations as the binding constraint on monetary policy, not growth.

Central bank communications from the past three months show a persistent hawkish bias: in March, the bank held rates steady despite 1.2% growth (normally a signal to cut), citing imported inflation and expectations risks, indicating that the 12.5% rate is a floor, not a ceiling, if commodity prices weaken.

Compare to 2021 when the central bank was cutting from 5.25% to 4.25% despite oil above $60: today's 12.5% with similar oil prices signals that the baseline risk scenario has shifted from manageable ruble weakness to potential currency crisis, justifying the hawkish stance.
expert: The policy rate at 12.5% implies a real rate (nominal minus expected inflation) of roughly 7.8%, assuming inflation expectations are anchored near 4.7% headline; survey evidence suggests expectations are actually 5.5-6.0%, implying a real rate of 6.5-7.0%, the highest in 15 years and consistent with recession-risk policy rates seen in 1998-1999.

The central bank's forward guidance in April 2026 signals 'patient' rate cuts beginning in Q4 2026 IF inflation stays below 5.0%, a conditional signal that implies the bank expects 25-50bps of cuts by year-end; however, this guidance is contingent on oil staying above $75, a condition with falling probability as OPEC+ production increases.

Watch the yield curve: at 140bps inverted (10Y yields 130bps below policy rate), the market is pricing a 50-75% probability of a recession and expects policy rates to fall to 8-9% by mid-2027; if the central bank cuts prematurely (above 100bps inversion), ruble weakness will force them back up, extending the policy rate at 12.5%+ through 2027 and pushing the growth forecast to negative.

beginner: Russia's stock market is down 1.1% year-to-date in ruble terms, which means if you invested in Russian stocks on January 1, you have lost money even though GDP is growing.

That does not match the usual story (stocks up when economy grows), because Russia's economy is growing from war spending and forced labor, not from businesses getting more profitable, so investors are skeptical.
The real indicator here is that smart money is not buying Russian stocks even in a growing economy, which signals that people do not believe growth is real or sustainable.
moderate: At 1.1% down in ruble terms year-to-date, the Russian stock market has underperformed both the central bank's 1.2% GDP growth and the 12.5% policy rate, indicating that equity investors expect either further depreciation or corporate profit compression from the combination of high rates and weak demand.

The market is heavily skewed toward energy stocks (Gazprom, Rosneft, Lukoil) and state-owned enterprises with guaranteed government contracts, while private sector industrials and consumer stocks are depressed, reflecting the bifurcation of the economy into war-beneficiary state firms and struggling private businesses.

Compare to 2022 when the stock market fell 50% in ruble terms following the invasion: the small 1.1% loss in 2026 looks resilient, but that reflects the low base and the dominance of state firms with administered valuations, not genuine investor confidence in Russian equities.
expert: The RTS Index (ruble-denominated) is down 1.1% YTD, driven by losses in energy (0.5% contribution) and weakness in consumer/industrial stocks (1.2% drag); this composition reveals that investors are rotating out of cyclical stocks and into defensive energy plays, anticipating demand slowdown.

Forward P/E ratios on Russian equities have compressed to 4.5-5.0x (Gazprom 3.2x, Sberbank 4.8x) compared to 8-10x pre-pandemic, indicating either deep undervaluation (unlikely given sanctions and geopolitical risk) or justifiable skepticism about earnings durability in a 1.2% growth regime.

Watch capital flows: if non-residents reduce holdings below 20% of market capitalization (currently 22-24%), the stock market will need ruble appreciation to attract domestic demand, a condition that only obtains if the central bank cuts rates below 10%, a move that will not come until inflation proves unambiguously below 4.0% (unlikely before Q4 2026).

beginner: Russia's 10-year government bond yield is at 13.5%, meaning if you lend Russia money for 10 years, the government will pay you 13.5% interest per year, roughly triple the policy rate of 12.5%.

That is a huge premium (the 10Y yield is usually lower than the short-term rate, not higher), and it signals that investors are terrified of default risk or currency collapse beyond 10 years, so they demand a punishing rate to take the risk.
If the 10Y yield falls below 11%, it means investors are getting less scared, which would be good news for Russia's ability to borrow; if it rises above 15%, it means a crisis is near.
moderate: The 10Y yield of 13.5% exceeds the policy rate of 12.5% by 100bps, a term premium that is historically elevated and reflects both inflation risk and an expectation that the central bank will be forced to cut rates below the long-term equilibrium (implying future currency depreciation or default risk).

Long-dated Russian debt is primarily held by domestic institutions (banks, pension funds) that are required or incentivized to hold government paper, not by foreign investors; the 13.5% yield is therefore not a true market-clearing price but an administered yield in a captive market.

Compare to 2021 when 10Y yields on Russian OFZs traded at 6.5-7.0%: the 13.5% yield today reflects a 550-700bps risk premium that corresponds to investor perceptions of Russia's geopolitical and fiscal sustainability risks; absent major de-escalation or sanctions relief, this premium will persist.
expert: The 10Y OFZ yield at 13.5% reflects a 100bps term premium over the 12.5% policy rate, a premium that is elevated relative to historical norms (typically 25-50bps in normal regimes) and signals market expectations of either policy rate cuts of 200-300bps over the 10-year horizon or default/restructuring probabilities priced at 5-10%.

Auction demand for 10Y OFZs in April 2026 shows bid-to-cover ratios of 1.5-1.8x (down from 3-4x in 2022-2023), indicating that even captive domestic demand is thinning and the central bank is absorbing an estimated 35-40% of new issuance directly, a Ponzi structure that is sustainable only if inflation remains below 5.0%.

If oil falls to $70 and the budget deficit widens to 4% of GDP, the Ministry of Finance will need to issue 300-350 billion rubles (roughly $4.5-5 billion) per quarter in new 10Y debt; if the central bank cannot expand purchases (because inflation is rising), yields will spike to 15.5-16.0% and trigger a credit crunch that collapses 1.2% growth to negative by Q3 2026.

beginner: The yield curve is inverted by 140 basis points, which means short-term interest rates are much higher than long-term rates, a pattern that normally happens only when a recession is coming.

A normal yield curve has long rates higher (you get paid more to lend money for 10 years than for 1 year), but Russia's is backwards because investors think there will be a crash soon and expect the central bank to cut rates.
Watch this: if the inversion gets worse (goes below 150bps), it means a crisis is expected within 6 months; if it flips to normal (positive slope), it means the worst fears are fading.
moderate: The yield curve inverted at 140bps (policy rate 12.5%, 10Y yield 13.5%) is unusual for Russia and reflects the market's expectation that a recession will force the central bank to cut rates by 200-250bps within the next two years, a cut that is only possible if inflation collapses or the economy enters free fall.

Normally, central banks flatten yield curves only when fighting inflation is the priority; today's curve is inverted not because of inflation control but because markets expect the central bank to abandon inflation fighting (by necessity) once growth turns negative, a reflexive devaluation and crisis scenario.

Compare to 2022 when the curve inverted briefly (100bps) during the initial sanctions shock: the recovery to a normal curve (positive slope of 50-100bps) took 12-18 months as growth stabilized and inflation fears subsided; today's 140bps inversion is deeper, suggesting greater recession risk and a longer period of high rates ahead.
expert: The yield curve at 140bps inverted (policy rate minus 10Y yield equals +1.4%) represents the deepest inversion since Q2 2022, consistent with a Fed policy rate inversion of 60-80bps seen in late 2022; this level of inversion prices a 50-65% probability of at least one policy rate cut of 50+bps within 12 months.

The inversion reflects a market-implied terminal rate path of 9.5-10.0% by end-2027 (versus current 12.5%), with the bulk of cuts (150-200bps) compressed into H2 2026-H1 2027; this path is only sustainable if inflation moderates to 3.5-4.0%, a condition that requires either oil to remain above $75 (low probability given OPEC+ signals) or demand to collapse (highly probable).

Watch for a flattening signal: if the inversion compresses to 80bps or less while oil stays above $75, the market will be pricing a soft landing (cuts without recession), and growth forecasts will revise upward; if the inversion deepens beyond 160bps, the market is pricing recession with inflation still sticky above 5%, and the next move will be a currency crisis and forced debt restructuring.

beginner: The ruble is trading at 76 to one US dollar, which means one ruble is worth 1.3 cents, a level that is weak compared to 2021 (70-75 to the dollar) but stable since 2023.

A weak ruble makes Russian exports cheaper and imports more expensive, which hurts ordinary people buying foreign goods but helps the government (since oil is sold in dollars) and helps companies that export.

The ruble has not collapsed (like Argentina or Lebanon's currencies have) because the central bank is keeping rates high and forcing companies to sell their dollars, which prevents the market from sending it much lower.
moderate: USD/RUB at 76.0 is 3-5% weaker than the 2021 average of 72-74 but 30% stronger than the 2022 post-invasion spike of 100-110, indicating that the ruble has recovered from acute crisis but remains in a weaker equilibrium reflecting geopolitical risk and capital controls.

The ruble is being defended by administrative measures (60% of export revenues must be surrendered to the central bank, capital outflows are restricted, and residents cannot hold foreign currency above threshold amounts), not by economic fundamentals; absent these controls, the fair value would be 85-95 to the dollar given the 12.5% yield advantage.

Compare to 2020 when USD/RUB was 73 with the policy rate at 4.25% and capital flows open: the 3-point depreciation today despite a 12.5% higher policy rate confirms that the ruble's weakness reflects expected depreciation (inflation expectations, geopolitical risk), not cyclical factors.
expert: USD/RUB at 76.0 with a policy rate of 12.5% implies an interest rate parity gap of 350-400bps (the ruble is overvalued by interest rate parity standards by 4-5%), a gap that is only maintained through capital controls, mandatory FX surrender requirements (50% of enterprise export earnings), and resident FX holding restrictions.

Fair value for USD/RUB absent capital controls is estimated at 82-88 based on real effective exchange rates and PPP; the 6-12 point undervaluation (current 76 versus fair 82-88) represents roughly $20-25 billion in economic rents to the central bank and the state, a transfer that suppresses private investment and consumption but sustains the 2.0% current account surplus.

If oil falls to $70 or below, the central bank's reserve inflow will slow and FX surrender requirements will become harder to enforce (exporters will find workarounds); a breach of 80 on USD/RUB with policy rates stuck at 12%+ will trigger capital flight expectations, forcing either a 150-200bps policy rate hike (growth negative) or a collapse past 90 (stagflation).

beginner: When you measure Russian stock market returns in US dollars instead of rubles, the return jumps from down 1.1% to up 2.33% year-to-date, which tells you that the ruble actually got a little bit stronger relative to the dollar over the first four months of 2026.

This difference matters if you are a foreign investor: you lost money on Russian stocks in ruble terms but made money when converted to dollars, a sign that the ruble strengthened just enough to offset the equity losses.

The fact that the ruble has held steady at 76 (not fallen to 80 or 85) is the only reason foreign investors have not taken even bigger losses, so watch the ruble closely: if it weakens, the USD return will turn negative even if the ruble return stays flat.
moderate: The 2.33% USD return versus the 1.1% ruble loss YTD implies a 3.4% ruble appreciation over the period, consistent with seasonal dollar strength (US rates remained high) combined with Russian capital controls keeping the ruble supported above fair value; the positive USD return masks deteriorating underlying equity fundamentals.

Foreign investors account for roughly 20-25% of Russian equity holdings, and the positive USD return has likely prevented further capital flight, a tail prop for the market; however, if the ruble weakens to 78-80 (a move that is probable if oil falls below $75), the USD return will turn negative 2-3%, triggering the outflow that the weak ruble has so far prevented.

Compare to 2022 when the ruble fell 30% (from 75 to 110 USD/RUB) even though the stock market fell 50% in ruble terms, producing a USD loss of 65%: today's 2.33% USD gain reflects both a stabilized ruble and a rebound off 2022's depressed valuations, not fundamental improvement in Russian equity prospects.
expert: The 2.33% USD return (RTS Index up 2.3% in rubles, ruble appreciated roughly 110bps against the dollar from Jan 1 to mid-April) reflects a rotation into energy and state-backed industrials that are less sensitive to ruble depreciation and more likely to benefit from oil revenues; the USD-ruble component contributed roughly 340bps of the total return.

Foreign investor flows into Russian equities have been flat to negative in 2026 (estimated 200-300 million dollars of net inflows, down from 1-2 billion annually in 2010-2015), indicating that the positive USD return is not attracting new capital but merely limiting outflows; the market is being sustained by domestic demand, primarily from compulsory pension fund allocations and captive insurance company holdings.

If oil falls to $70 and the ruble weakens past 78 (pushing USD/RUB returns negative), foreign investor momentum will turn decisively negative; combined with domestic supply increases (forced sales by companies with FX exposure), a 10-15% USD decline in Russian equities over 2-3 quarters is probable, a downside that will fully materialize if the central bank cuts rates below 11% before inflation reaches 3.5%.

beginner: Higher oil prices could boost Russia's economy, but they would also give the Kremlin more cash to fund the war in Ukraine. This is not good for Russia's neighbors or for global stability.
Russia's growth is expected to slow to 0.8% next year because of sanctions, not because of oil prices. The economy is grinding down under the weight of military spending and isolation.
CPI at 6% and policy rate at 15.5% show inflation is real and the central bank is fighting hard. But this tightness will not fix the structural damage from war and sanctions.
moderate: Rising oil prices offer Russia a temporary windfall, but the Kremlin will spend it on the war in Ukraine, not on investment or growth. The forecast of 0.8% growth in 2026 reflects this reality: sanctions, capital flight, and military spending drain the economy faster than higher oil revenues can help. CPI at 6.01% and policy rate at 15.5% signal the central bank is fighting inflation but losing, because the ruble is weak and import costs are rising.

Unemployment at 2.15% looks tight, but it reflects military conscription and emigration, not strength. The policy rate at 15.5% is the highest in the dataset and signals desperation, not confidence. Compare this to Brazil's 15%: Brazil is fighting inflation in a market economy with functioning institutions. Russia is using rates as a war finance tool.

Watch energy prices and capital outflows. If crude sustains above $75 and Russia captures the windfall, it extends the war timeline and the pain for neighbors. If crude falls or Russia faces new sanctions on energy, the 0.8% growth forecast is too optimistic and the economy contracts. Either way, Russia's isolation deepens.
expert: CPI at 6.01% in January and policy rate at 15.5% in February mask a fundamental problem: the ruble is depreciating, capital is fleeing, and the central bank is rationing credit to prop up the military-industrial complex. The 2.15% unemployment rate reflects conscription and emigration, not labor market tightness. Oil prices at $75-80/bbl provide a cash windfall that the Kremlin will deploy to the war, not to productive investment.

Directional signal: growth is decelerating structurally. The 0.8% forecast for 2026 assumes some stabilization in demand and capital controls holding. If new US or EU sanctions target energy (the 40% of government revenue), or if capital outflows accelerate, growth turns negative. The policy rate at 15.5% is already at war-time levels and cannot go much higher without inducing a credit crunch.

Forward implication: watch crude prices and US sanctions announcements. If crude stays above $80 and new sanctions are delayed, Russia muddles through 2026 with near-zero growth, high inflation, and steady capital flight. If sanctions target energy exports or target the central bank directly, the ruble crashes, inflation spikes above 10%, and the 0.8% forecast becomes minus 2%. The war timeline is now pegged to oil prices and geopolitical risk, not to economic fundamentals.

fxRegime.label: Managed Float (Capital Controls)
fxRegime.beginner: Russia's ruble is officially a 'floating' currency, but in practice the government heavily controls it. After Western sanctions froze Russia's foreign reserves in 2022, Moscow imposed strict rules: exporters must convert most of their foreign earnings into rubles, and there are limits on how much money can leave the country. USD/RUB shows how many rubles one US dollar buys. At 81, one dollar costs 81 rubles — much stronger than the 110+ level seen in late 2024, but this strength is largely engineered by capital controls rather than genuine market confidence.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float with extensive capital controls imposed post-2022 sanctions. The CBR intervenes indirectly via mandatory FX conversion requirements (80% of export proceeds) rather than direct market operations, since ~$300bn of reserves remain frozen in Western jurisdictions. The onshore USD/RUB rate (~81) diverges from offshore NDF pricing, reflecting convertibility risk and sanctions premium. Ruble volatility is artificially suppressed by capital controls but subject to periodic dislocations when enforcement changes or oil price shocks hit. The effective FX regime is closer to a managed peg maintained by administrative measures rather than reserve-based intervention.
fxRegime.expert: De facto dual exchange rate regime masked as a managed float. Onshore rate (~81/USD) is administratively managed via: (1) mandatory 80% FX conversion for exporters; (2) restrictions on cross-border capital transfers; (3) informal 'guidance' to state-owned banks on FX positioning. Offshore NDF market (thin liquidity, wide bid-ask) reflects true risk-adjusted convertibility value. The 45% appreciation in 2025 is a policy choice — it contains imported inflation and signals stability, but at the cost of fiscal revenue compression (each 1 RUB appreciation costs ~₽150bn in annual oil revenue) and export competitiveness erosion. The CBR's usable reserves (~$250bn after subtracting frozen assets and gold held domestically) provide limited ammunition for genuine intervention; the regime's stability depends entirely on capital control enforcement and commodity price levels.

GDP Growth.beginner: Russia's economy has been kept running largely by military spending and energy revenues, but with the shadow fleet of tankers under increasing pressure and the ongoing cost of the Ukraine war, Russia's longer-term economic sustainability remains questionable.
GDP Growth.moderate: Russia's GDP growth (officially positive, driven by defence spending and wartime production) benefits from higher oil revenues at $90+ Urals-equivalent, but the economy's structural distortions — inflation, labor shortages from mobilisation, sanctioned technology gaps — mean higher oil prices mask rather than resolve the underlying fragility.
GDP Growth.expert: Russia's fiscal breakeven at ~$70-80/barrel Urals means current prices are above breakeven, providing National Wealth Fund breathing room; but Russian economic data is severely impaired by wartime opacity, and independent estimates suggest significant misallocation: military production crowds out civilian investment, inflation is above the CBR's 4% target, and real wages in the civilian economy are being eroded by defence-sector demand for labour.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Russia's inflation has been high, well above the central bank's 4% target, pushed up by government spending on the war, sanctions limiting imported goods, and a weakening ruble — and the Iran conflict adds further uncertainty.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Russian CPI has been running materially above the CBR's 4% target (estimated 8-12% depending on methodology) due to wartime fiscal expansion, import substitution failures, and ruble depreciation; the Iran conflict creates contradictory forces — higher oil revenues are ruble-positive (reducing import inflation) but global risk-off could weaken the ruble via capital flight.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Russia's inflation measurement is methodologically compromised by wartime price controls, the disappearance of sanctioned product categories from the CPI basket, and the divergence between official and black-market exchange rates; the FRED series for Russian CPI (RUSCPIALLMINMEI) remains active and provides one of the few internationally benchmarked data points, but its reliability as a measure of ordinary Russians' cost-of-living experience is increasingly questioned by independent economists.

Unemployment.beginner: Russia's official unemployment is very low — near historic lows — but this is misleading; many workers have been drafted into the military, and severe labour shortages in civilian industries are pushing up wages in ways that fuel inflation.
Unemployment.moderate: Russia's reported unemployment near 2.5% reflects military mobilisation absorbing civilian workers, not genuine full employment; the labour shortage in civilian manufacturing, logistics, and agriculture is generating double-digit wage inflation in some sectors that is contributing to above-target CPI and complicating the CBR's inflation management.
Unemployment.expert: Russia's labour market is distorted by the largest military mobilisation since WWII: approximately 600,000-800,000 troops deployed creates a structural labour supply reduction in civilian industries; the resulting wage pressure in civilian sectors (construction, agriculture, logistics) represents a form of forced supply-side constraint that resembles an adverse labour supply shock — distinct from demand-side dynamics that conventional monetary policy can address.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Russia's government is spending heavily on its military operations, and while high oil prices help fund this, the costs of the Ukraine war are draining the country's savings and creating long-term fiscal pressures.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Russia's oil revenues at above-breakeven Urals prices reduce the pace of National Wealth Fund depletion; however, military spending (estimated at 6-7% of GDP officially, possibly higher including classified items) creates a structural deficit that is only sustainable if oil prices remain elevated and the NWF maintains sufficient liquidity.
Budget Deficit.expert: Russia's fiscal position is uniquely sensitive to the Urals-Brent discount: Western sanctions and shadow fleet logistics costs have historically maintained a $10-20 discount; if the Iran conflict increases global tanker demand and reduces shadow fleet operating freedom (US naval presence, increased insurance scrutiny), the effective discount could widen even as Brent rises, compressing Russia's net oil revenue despite headline oil price strength.

Current Account.beginner: Russia earns significant revenue from selling oil and gas to China, India, and other countries that have not joined Western sanctions, and higher oil prices mean more income coming into the country — though the shadow tanker fleet faces increasing scrutiny.
Current Account.moderate: Russia's current account has recovered from post-invasion lows as the shadow fleet enabled continued oil exports at discounted Urals prices; at current price levels, the current account surplus is meaningful, but the Iran conflict introduces uncertainty about the shadow fleet's operational freedom if the US military's Gulf presence intensifies enforcement of secondary sanctions.
Current Account.expert: Russia's oil export supply chain depends critically on the shadow tanker fleet (estimated 700+ vessels) enabling price-cap-circumventing sales to India and China; the Iran conflict creates several risk vectors: US secondary sanction enforcement may intensify as part of Middle East campaign strategic logic; insurers may become more restrictive about shadow fleet coverage; and Indian state refiners may be constrained in increasing Russian imports while managing their own energy supply emergency — all potentially compressing Russia's realised export volumes and prices.

Policy Rate.beginner: Russia's central bank has kept interest rates very high to try to control inflation caused by military spending and the economic distortions of sanctions, but high rates are also hurting Russian businesses that need to borrow to invest.
Policy Rate.moderate: The CBR's policy rate (likely 16-21% based on recent history; FRED data available) is set in a wartime context where conventional monetary transmission is impaired: high rates are intended to control inflation and defend the ruble, but the military spending impulse is itself inflationary and not rate-sensitive, making the CBR's task difficult in both theory and practice.
Policy Rate.expert: Russia's monetary policy operates in a command-economy hybrid: the CBR has maintained de jure independence but faces political pressure to balance war-financing needs (lower rates for state banks funding defence contracts) with inflation control (high rates) and ruble stability (high rates); the effective transmission of policy rate changes is severely impaired by the prevalence of subsidised state credit for defence-related production — creating a dual-rate economy where headline CBR rates reflect anti-inflation intent but actual financing conditions for strategic industries are materially lower.

moderate: WTI Crude at $90.90/barrel (+36% WoW) and Brent at $92.69 (+27%) reflect acute Strait of Hormuz disruption: ~140 million barrels of regional crude is stranded, OPEC+ announced a larger-than-expected production increase but barrels are largely inaccessible given the shipping halt; analysts warn Brent could exceed $100 if the conflict lasts beyond 4 weeks.

Gold at $5,158/oz continues its multi-year bull run, now compounded by the Iran conflict flight-to-safety bid; the metal benefits simultaneously from central bank buying (EM reserve diversification), USD weakness earlier in 2026, and an acute geopolitical risk premium; silver at $84.31 is tracking higher on both safe-haven and industrial demand.

Agricultural commodities are rising as the Middle East conflict disrupts shipping: wheat (+5.8% weekly) faces a dual shock: the Middle East is a large wheat importer and key shipping routes are disrupted; soybeans (+3.2%) are supported by China's continued import demand and Brazilian export strength; corn (+4.3%) reflects biofuel demand as energy prices spike globally.
expert: The WTI/Brent spread has narrowed to ~$1.79 (from a typical $3-5), reflecting the global nature of the supply shock and US SPR release speculation: with approximately 9mb/d off the market from facility damage and precautionary shutdowns, and OPEC+ production geographically constrained by Hormuz closure, the market's clearing mechanism is IEA strategic reserve coordination, a tool that buys weeks, not months, of price suppression.

Gold's rally above $5,100 represents a regime shift in the gold-real-rate relationship: previously gold tracked inversely to US real rates (TIPS yields); the current gold strength despite higher real rates (driven by CPI upside from energy) suggests the safe-haven bid is overriding the rate-discount mechanism, a pattern historically associated with tail-risk scenarios where the monetary policy reaction function itself becomes uncertain.

Agricultural commodity supercycle dynamics are being reinforced by the Iran shock: fertiliser (natural gas-intensive in production) prices are spiking with LNG, creating a second-order agricultural supply shock for the 2026/2027 growing season; the FAO food price index is likely to reverse its recent moderation; and the combination of energy and food price inflation in a single shock is historically the most damaging inflation configuration for EM sovereign credit.

commentary.beginner: Commodities are the raw materials that power the global economy - things like oil, gold, wheat, and copper. Their prices affect everything from the cost of filling your car to the price of bread. When oil rises, transport gets more expensive, which pushes up prices across the board. Gold often rises when people are worried about the economy.
commentary.moderate: Commodity markets are signalling mixed conditions. Energy prices remain subdued on soft China demand and resilient US shale supply, while gold continues to rally on central bank buying and safe-haven demand. Agricultural commodities are pressured by strong Southern Hemisphere harvests. The copper-to-gold ratio - a classic growth proxy - has been declining, consistent with a slowing global cycle.
commentary.expert: Cross-commodity signal extraction: the backwardation in crude (WTI M1-M6 spread ~$1.80) suggests physical tightness despite flat prices, consistent with OPEC+ compliance above 90%. Gold's move above $2,900 is driven less by real rates (still positive) and more by EM central bank reserve diversification (PBOC, RBI, NBP cumulative buying ~1,100t in 2024-25). Dr. Copper's sideways action reflects offsetting forces: China property drag vs. electrification pull. The GSCI/SPX ratio near 40-year lows signals extreme undervaluation of real assets vs. financial assets.
